title: Asymptotic Cones and the Sublinear Triangle Criterion

items.title: Rescaled ultralimits and asymptotic cones
items.statement: For a fixed free ultrafilter on N, pointed metric spaces (X_n,e_n), and positive lambda_n, use sequences with sup_n lambda_n d_n(x_n,e_n)<infinity. Declare x~y when lim_omega lambda_n d_n(x_n,y_n)=0 and give the quotient the ultradistance. A cone has X_n=X and lambda_n tending to zero in the ordinary sense. Definitions are provisional until the next two lemmas. Sequences bounded only omega-almost everywhere give the same quotient by replacing exceptional coordinates by e_n.

items.title: Free tail ultrafilters and bounded real ultralimit calculus
items.statement: Under AC there is a free ultrafilter on N. For a supplied ultrafilter every bounded real sequence has a unique ultralimit, preserving sums, scalar products, order and absolute value. The latter assertions require no new choice.
items.strategy: Use the choice-free least-upper-bound conclusion of cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete. Its published Cauchy-completeness supplier now constructs rational approximants by unique least natural triples (height, positive denominator, shifted numerator), using earlier well-ordering, integer/rational representations, Cartesian product and Separation; it does not choose representatives of a sequence of reals or import the later rational-countability theorem. Before using that completeness interface, discharge the reciprocal step in its real-field prerequisite locally: for a non-null rational Cauchy sequence a, lem-cauchy-away-from-zero gives rational delta>0 and N0>=1 with |a_n|>delta for n>=N0. Define b_n=1 before N0 and b_n=1/a_n thereafter. For rational epsilon>0 take N at least N0 and a Cauchy index for a at epsilon delta^2. For m,n>=N, rational ordered-field arithmetic and lem-rat-triangle give |b_m-b_n|=|a_m-a_n|/(|a_m||a_n|)<=|a_m-a_n|/delta^2<epsilon, including a_m=a_n. Thus b belongs to the Cauchy ring. The sequence ab-1 is eventually zero, hence null by def-null-sequence. By thm-cauchy-ring and lem-null-ideal, every ideal containing the null ideal and a contains 1=ab-(ab-1), so it is the whole ring; the null ideal is proper and therefore maximal. This is a complete local replacement for the false strict intermediate inequality at lem-null-maximal proof 3.1; the replacement uses only the six explicitly declared earlier rational/Cauchy suppliers, not lem-null-maximal or real completeness. Its conclusion discharges that exact input of the published real-field construction and hence of the completeness interface used here. The supersets of tails form a proper filter. Extend it by the published AC-based ultrafilter lemma; a finite set cannot belong because its complementary tail does. Bisect a closed bounded interval containing the sequence, at each stage selecting the left half if its preimage is large, otherwise the right half. The supremum of the left endpoints is the unique intersection point: lengths tend to zero by the Archimedean consequence of ordered-field completeness, proved locally by applying a supremum argument to the natural numbers. Every epsilon-neighbourhood contains a chosen interval. Intersect the finitely many large sets for epsilon estimates to prove uniqueness, sum, scalar, order and absolute-value rules. This construction is deterministic once omega is supplied; it does not use countable choice by induction.

items.title: The rescaled ultradistance defines a metric
items.statement: On the bounded sequence space, zero ultradistance is an equivalence relation and the ultradistance induces a finite genuine metric on its quotient. Modification off an omega-large set does not change a point.
items.strategy: Bound pairwise distances by the two distances to e_n. Pass symmetry and triangle inequalities through the bounded-real calculus; nonnegativity follows from 0=d(x,x)<=2d(x,y). For representatives x~xprime,y~yprime, bound the absolute difference of the pairwise distances by d(x,xprime)+d(y,yprime). Separation is precisely the quotient relation. Coordinates on an exceptional set may all be replaced by the supplied basepoints. No choice and no completion theorem is needed.

items.title: Oriented geodesic rays, lines, parameters and tails
items.statement: In a geodesic metric space, an oriented geodesic ray is an isometric embedding rho:[0,infinity)->X, with origin rho(0), parameter t and image rho([0,infinity)); its T-tail is rho([T,infinity)). An oriented geodesic line is an isometric embedding ell:R->X, with signed parameter t, orientation t increasing, and positive and negative tails ell([T,infinity)) and ell((-infinity,-T]). These are maps, not merely their images; reversing a line reverses its orientation. A common tail means equality of ray images after specified nonnegative parameter thresholds, and finite Hausdorff distance is always between images.

items.title: Limits of geodesic segments, rays and lines
items.statement: Assume AC. Ultralimits of pointed geodesic spaces are geodesic. A sequence of oriented segments meeting a bounded rescaled neighbourhood of the basepoints has a limit isometric to a closed interval, ray or line, with endpoints determined by the limiting distances from chosen origins. Every bounded sequence of points on these segments lies on this parameterized limit. The parameter origins o_n must lie in one uniformly bounded rescaled neighbourhood of e_n on the large set; use e_n on exceptional coordinates.
items.strategy: For every supplied segment meeting an R-bounded rescaled neighbourhood of the basepoint, use AC to choose a witness o_n there and center an oriented original-distance geodesic gamma_n at o_n. Write its ORIGINAL parameter interval as [-alpha_n,beta_n], where alpha_n,beta_n>=0. Define RESCALED endpoints a_n=lambda_n alpha_n and b_n=lambda_n beta_n. The origin has bounded rescaled distance from the cone basepoint. The extended nonnegative ultralimits a,b exist by applying bounded-real ultralimit calculus to a_n/(1+a_n), b_n/(1+b_n); limit 1 means the corresponding endpoint is infinite. For finite t in the limiting interval [-a,b], put c_n(t)=max(-a_n,min(t,b_n)) and x_n(t)=gamma_n(c_n(t)/lambda_n). Thus clamping is in rescaled units and division by lambda_n occurs only when evaluating the original-distance geodesic. The endpoint limits imply lim_omega c_n(t)=t, including finite endpoints and either infinite direction. Also |c_n(t)|<=|t|, so x_n(t) is an admissible cone sequence. The exact identity lambda_n d(x_n(s),x_n(t))=|c_n(s)-c_n(t)| gives limiting distance |s-t| and hence an isometric parameterization. Conversely, a represented sequence z_n on the segment has a signed ORIGINAL parameter u_n and bounded RESCALED parameter t_n=lambda_n u_n, since its distance to o_n is rescaled-bounded. Let t=lim_omega t_n; then -a<=t<=b. Because t_n lies in [-a_n,b_n], projection to that interval gives |t_n-c_n(t)|<=|t_n-t|. The rescaled distance from z_n to x_n(t) tends to zero, so both represent the same cone point. This proves the entire represented-side assertion, not just the endpoints. Finite, one-infinite and two-infinite limiting endpoints give respectively a closed interval (possibly a point), an oriented ray, and a line. For cone geodesicity choose original segments joining any two representative sequences, with the first endpoint as o_n; their rescaled lengths tend to the cone distance, and the constructed limit segment joins the two represented endpoints. AC is used only for the countable families of original geodesics and bounded-neighbourhood witnesses; clamping and all parameter conversions are explicit.

items.title: Real trees, tripod triangles, slimness and minsize
items.statement: A real tree is a geodesic metric space with a unique topological arc between every two distinct points. An arc is, by definition, the image of a homeomorphism [0,1]->A; when a continuous injective parametrization is supplied, [0,1] is compact by thm-heine-borel-r, its metric image is Hausdorff by thm-metric-hausdorff-separation, and thm-metric-continuity-characterisations plus thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps make the parametrization a homeomorphism onto its image. A tripod triangle is three intervals glued at one common endpoint, allowing zero legs. For three chosen geodesic sides define slimness as the maximum over their points of the distance to the other two sides; define minsize as the minimum diameter of a triple with one point on each side. For a nonempty geodesic metric space X and P>=0, let m_X(P) be the supremum of minsize over all chosen triangles of perimeter at most P, including the degenerate triangle at each point. Define delta-slimness and hyperbolicity locally. Hausdorff distance is max of the two directed suprema of infimum distances. No later HG item is imported. The triangle minsize is at most its perimeter, so 0<=m_X(P)<=P and the supremum is finite; m_X is intentionally not defined for an empty space.

items.title: Triangle extrema and the tripod and branch rules for real trees
items.statement: Minsize and slimness attain their extrema on any fixed finite triangle. In a geodesic space unique arcs, all triangles being tripods, and all chosen triangles being 0-slim are equivalent. In a tree, rays with a common origin at finite Hausdorff distance coincide; two lines at finite Hausdorff distance coincide; rays at finite Hausdorff distance have common tails.
items.strategy: The compact-interval/homeomorphism interface is the one declared by def-real-tree-tripods-and-geodesic-triangle-minsize. For extremizing sequences, enumerate rational grids on the finitely many parameter intervals and choose the first point within 2^{-n} of the infimum or supremum. Lipschitz continuity makes these grids sufficient; this avoids an unstated countable choice. Distance to a nonempty set is 1-Lipschitz. On a finite product of closed bounded intervals, repeated bisection gives a convergent subsequence of any sequence and hence extrema of continuous functions, including diameter and distance to compact sides. For tripod triangles, segments from an origin have intersection an initial closed interval; separation and reconnection would give a nontripod triangle. At an interior point p of [x,y], partition the complement by whether two geodesics toward p share a positive final segment. Tripods prove transitivity and show each class open: a ball of radius d(z,p) stays in its class. The classes containing x and y differ. To justify the path-separation step using the declared least-upper-bound supplier, suppose a continuous path on [0,1] avoids p. The inverse images U of the class containing x and V of the union of the other classes are disjoint relatively open sets covering [0,1], with 0 in U and 1 in V. Let s be the supremum of t with [0,t] contained in U. Openness near 0 and 1 gives 0<s<1, and every t<s lies in U. If s belongs to V, a left neighbourhood contradicts this; if s belongs to U, a right neighbourhood extends the initial interval beyond s, again a contradiction. Thus every continuous path x to y contains p; no later connectedness or recorded separation theorem is used. An injective path then equals [x,y]. Conversely, two different routes in a triangle would give two arcs with the same endpoints, so unique arcs force a tripod. For 0-slim triangles, a degenerate triangle consisting of two choices of the same segment proves uniqueness; intersection intervals then give tripods. With the oriented domains and tails of def-geodesic-rays-and-lines, two rays that split have distances growing by the sum of the tails; two lines or finite-Hausdorff rays reduce to this fact by cutting at the specified common or nearest joining segment. Record the finite/one-infinite/two-infinite endpoint versions explicitly.

items.title: Tree cones force uniform control of sides with a common endpoint
items.statement: Assume AC and fix one free ultrafilter omega. If Cone_omega(X,e,lambda) is a real tree for every basepoint sequence and every positive lambda_n tending to zero, there is M>0 such that d_H([x,y],[x,z])<=M d(y,z) whenever d(y,z)>1, for all choices of the two segments.
items.strategy: Otherwise choose triangles with ratios M_n>n, exchange y,z when needed, and choose a maximizing point a_n on [x_n,y_n]. Put D_n=d(a_n,[x_n,z_n])=d_H and scale by 1/D_n; D_n>n. Both side limits exist, are at Hausdorff distance at most one, and distance of a=[a_n] to the other is exactly one. Since d(y_n,z_n)/D_n tends to zero, the far endpoints either converge to the same point or both escape. The common x_n endpoint is either finite or escapes. The parameterized-limit lemma makes the sides, respectively, segments with the same endpoints, rays with the same finite endpoint, or two lines. Finite Hausdorff distance contradicts the appropriate tree rule in all three cases. AC chooses violating triangles and maxima; no properness of X is assumed.

items.title: Tree cones at all basepoints and scales imply uniform slimness
items.statement: Under AC, if every basepoint/scaling cone for one fixed free ultrafilter is a real tree, all geodesic triangles in X are delta-slim for some finite delta depending on X.
items.strategy: Choose triangles whose maximum side-to-opposite-sides distance d_n>n is attained at a_n on [x_n,y_n], with nearest b_n on [y_n,z_n]. Choose nearest c_n on [x_n,z_n], put D_n=d(a_n,c_n)>=d_n, and base/scale at a_n,1/d_n. The maximum must be over all three sides, not only the first. If D_n/d_n has finite ultralimit, a,b,c survive. Two-side control applied to each of the endpoint-matched half-sides pairs their limits into segments or asymptotic rays (first extend two-side control to d_H<=C max(1,d(y,z)): if d(y,z)<=1 and [x,y] has length >=3, shorten it by 3 at y; the new endpoint is at distance between 2 and 4 from z, so the bound is 3+4M; if its length is <3, both sides have length <4. Take C=4M+4). The resulting finite/ideal triangle in the tree is a tripod, contradicting distance one of a from the other sides. If D_n/d_n tends to infinity, the entire third side disappears locally and x_n,z_n escape. Control pairs the halves toward y_n. Global maximality forces every bounded point of the half-side from b_n toward z_n to lie within one of the first side in the limit. Thus the two surviving rays with common origin, or lines with matched ends, are distinct but at finite Hausdorff distance, impossible by the tree rules. Spell out half-line orientation with signed parameters; no compactness of X or undefined ideal boundary theorem is used.

items.title: Sublinear minsize identifies every cone segment with a limit segment
items.statement: Assume AC and let X be a nonempty geodesic metric space with m_X(P)=o(P). In any cone, for any endpoints represented by a_n,b_n and any chosen segments [a_n,b_n], their limit is the unique segment between the endpoint classes.
items.strategy: Take c on an arbitrary cone segment and a representative c_n; choose the other two segments of the representative triangle. Its perimeter P_n satisfies lambda_n P_n bounded. For every epsilon, minsize<=epsilon P_n for P_n sufficiently large, whereas on bounded P_n use minsize<=P_n and lambda_n tending to zero. Hence lambda_n minsize tends to zero. Minimizing triples x_n on [a_n,b_n], y_n on [a_n,c_n], z_n on [c_n,b_n] have a common limit x. Distance identities give d(a,b)<=d(a,x)+d(x,b)<=d(a,x)+d(x,b)+2d(x,c)=d(a,c)+d(c,b)=d(a,b); thus x=c. The segment-limit parameterization shows containment is equality, since each distance parameter from a occurs exactly once. AC chooses representative side families, not a simultaneously privileged geodesic in every cone.

items.title: Sublinear triangle minsize implies hyperbolicity
items.statement: Assume AC. Every nonempty geodesic metric space with m_X(P)/P tending to zero as P tends to infinity has a finite uniform slimness constant. The empty space is separately and vacuously delta-slim for every delta, but no m_X profile is assigned to it.
items.strategy: Every cone is geodesic; the preceding lemma makes it uniquely geodesic and makes every chosen triangle a limit triangle. Representative minimizing triples coalesce, so all three sides meet. Unique geodesicity makes their intersections initial intervals and their union a tripod. Apply the tree-cone theorem. All basepoints and all scales are quantified; a single cone is insufficient.

items.title: Bounded-edge coarse fillings of loops and triangles
items.statement: A coarse disk is a finite combinatorial triangulation of a topological closed disk with a map of vertices into X; images of adjacent vertices have distance at most r>0, and the boundary map is the restriction of the vertex map in cyclic order. Exact fillings match a prescribed list entry-for-entry; fillings up to inserted repetitions match its expansion into positive consecutive blocks of each prescribed occurrence. A length-zero walk at x uses the singleton list (x); marked refinements retain corner occurrences and each arc image set. Area is its number N of triangles, counted even when their image degenerates. For a boundary marked in three consecutive arcs, coarse minsize is the minimum diameter of one mapped boundary vertex from each arc. Algebraic relator area retains the earlier finite-presentation convention. Interior vertices and triangles need not map continuously into X; only their subsequent coordinate maps to R^2 are extended affinely.

items.title: Singular planar labelled relator diagrams and their outer walks
items.statement: Fix P=<X|R>. A singular planar labelled relator diagram is a finite connected plane combinatorial 2-complex: its 1-skeleton is an embedded finite multigraph, allowing loops and parallel edges, and its face interiors are open polygon images disjoint from the entire embedded 1-skeleton and from one another, attached along cyclic finite edge-occurrence walks, with all incidences counted with multiplicity. An oriented edge has a label in X union X^{-1}, and reversal has the inverse label; each face walk reads a cyclic conjugate of a relator or its inverse. The outer boundary walk is the cyclic occurrence walk adjacent to the unbounded complementary region, with bridges traversed twice and with all excursions at a cut vertex taken in their plane cyclic order. A thin edge is incident with no relator face; a bridge is an edge whose deletion disconnects the 1-skeleton; a cut vertex has the analogous deletion property. The diagram is contractible when its plane carrier contracts to a point, including the one-vertex zero-face diagram. A Cayley vertex labelling is a map V-><X|R> for which an oriented edge labelled x from v to w has label(w)=label(v)x. The outer word and each face word are read from their oriented occurrences, so loops, monogons, bigons, repeated vertices and repeated boundary occurrences are data rather than suppressed pictures. The plane has its standard orientation; the literal outer walk keeps the unbounded region locally on its left and starts at a specified directed edge occurrence.

items.title: Finite polygonal disk parametrizations and boundary surgery
items.statement: All polygonal terminology here means finitely many straight segments with disjoint interiors, except shared endpoints. A simple polygon bounds a closed disk; a prescribed piecewise-linear boundary identification with another polygon extends to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism of the closed disks, with a piecewise-linear inverse after finite subdivisions. No extension to the ambient plane is asserted or needed. A finite embedded arc has a disk neighbourhood built from vertex disks and edge strips. A finite connected plane graph has a compact planar disk-and-band neighbourhood; capping all its bounded complementary boundary circles gives a closed disk. Subdividing an edge does not alter these assertions; loops contribute two distinct germs at their vertex.
items.strategy: Prove the finite polygon assertions here, not by the recorded Jordan theorem or the later plane-graph page. Rotate coordinates to separate the finitely many vertex abscissae. The vertical slabs split into trapezoids. Tracing the oriented polygon lists all left-side trapezoids in a connected cyclic sequence and likewise all right-side trapezoids. Crossing parity is unchanged across a slab wall (the number above changes by zero or two), and opposite across an edge. Thus the two sequences give precisely two complementary components, only the outside one unbounded. An extreme convex corner supplies an internal diagonal: use the segment joining its neighbours if its triangle contains no other vertex, and otherwise the segment to the vertex furthest toward the corner in that triangle. No edge can cross the chosen segment without an endpoint further toward the corner. Remove collinear corners first and restore them by boundary subdivision. Inductively splitting along diagonals triangulates the inside. The same noncrossing diagonals on a convex polygon have the same incidence pattern, so affine maps on corresponding triangles give a disk parametrization. For a prescribed PL boundary map f between two polygonal disks P1,P2, take the triangulation maps h1,h2 from them to convex polygons C1,C2. The map h2 f h1^-1 of their boundaries is PL. Insert all its breakpoints, all polygon corners and all inverse images of target corners. Choose interior points c1,c2 and cone each consecutive boundary subinterval to its center. Both are finite triangulations because the polygons are convex. Map c1 to c2 and corresponding boundary vertices to each other, affinely on each fan triangle. The triangles have disjoint interiors, cover their respective disks, and are matched in cyclic order; their affine maps agree on seams and their inverses do likewise. This gives a PL disk homeomorphism with exactly the prescribed boundary map. Composing with h1 and h2^-1 stays PL: intersect the finitely many image triangles with the next triangulation, pull back the resulting convex polygon cells and triangulate them. Collinear boundary subdivision points cause no degeneracy in the cone triangles since their centers are strictly interior. This proves finite PL control, not merely topological invertibility. It uses embedded simple polygons only; there is no annulus cut or doubled slit boundary. For the arc neighbourhood, choose mutually disjoint small polygonal vertex disks and disjoint narrow strips on each open segment; make finitely many smaller choices near bends. Along a path, attach one strip and the next disk across single boundary intervals. Two disks joined along one boundary interval are a disk: parametrize them as upper/lower half-disks and glue their diameters. Induction gives the asserted arc disk and also permits a prescribed parameter along either shore. For a graph the same disks and strips form a compact planar surface with boundary: interior points of a seam have two half-disk charts, corner points have a finite sector chart, and the distinct attachment intervals prevent singular vertices, also at loops. Its boundary is a disjoint finite collection of simple polygons. Connectedness gives a unique outer boundary; each other boundary encloses a complementary hole by the already proved polygon separation. Capping every inner boundary fills all holes and leaves exactly the closed inside of the outer polygon, hence a disk by the parametrization above. A bounded face with a repeated vertex is handled by its distinct boundary occurrences on the neighbourhood, not by claiming the original face frontier is an embedded circle. All selections are finite. This lemma supplies topology only; triangle counts are proved separately.

items.title: Relator expressions admit singular planar diagrams with controlled incidence
items.statement: For a word w of length n with an expression using m relator conjugates of lengths at most L, there is a def-singular-planar-labelled-relator-diagram with outer boundary w, at most m relator faces and total number of edges E<=Lm+n. Every non-face edge is thin, a bridge, and is traversed twice by the outer walk; every other edge has a face incidence. Its Cayley vertex labelling is consistent. This is a local supplier, not an invocation of the published closed-disk van Kampen definition.
items.strategy: Use the finite polygonal disk/collar lemma throughout. Draw a planar lollipop for a given m-factor expression; each relator disk and connecting whisker is added in its own exterior sector. It has m faces, total relator incidence I<=Lm, and all bounded complementary graph regions filled. Keep a characteristic polygon for each face, injective on its open interior. Each occupied side of each open graph edge corresponds to exactly one side occurrence in exactly one characteristic polygon; the opposite side may belong to that same polygon. Face-side occurrences are never replaced by an assumption of an embedded closed face boundary. Each face interior is one bounded complementary graph region, and all bounded regions are occupied. These invariants hold for lollipops. Give Cayley labels by partial products. Empty relators can be omitted. Reduce its literal outer word, preserving these invariants. Here is the precise distinct-endpoints fold for two consecutive boundary edges that form a simple arc. A thin exterior collar supplies a simple triangular disk T meeting the carrier exactly in those two edges. Construct a containing polygonal disk N by a positive-width exterior notch, as follows. Take a large rectangle R around the carrier and T. Join the interior of T's third side to R through the unbounded complementary region by a simple polygonal path, disjoint from T except its starting point; a generic path with loops erased suffices. Its sufficiently narrow strip, widened at its first end to attach along the whole third side of T and at its last end to an interval J of R, has two distinct disjoint shores. Finite vertex disks and strips construct this notch, with its interior disjoint from the carrier and T. No zero-width slit is used. The boundary consisting of R minus the interior of J, the two notch shores and T's third side is an embedded simple polygon. Its closed inside N contains the carrier and T. Removing T's interior replaces that third side by the two folding sides, again producing an embedded simple polygon K; its inside is the closure of N minus T. In particular T and K are genuine polygonal disks meeting exactly in the simple two-edge folding arc, not abstract cut-annulus surfaces. Map T to T0={|x|<=y<=1}, prescribing the two edge parameters (-t,t) and (t,t), and map K to the closure of R0 minus T0, where R0=[-2,2]x[-1,1]. Their boundary maps agree on the shared two-edge arc; choose the complementary boundary maps monotonically and PL with all required corners and breakpoints. The finite PL disk-extension lemma supplies both maps. They glue to a PL homeomorphism N to R0 with PL inverse by the same finite triangle refinement. Only this map restricted to the carrier is used: no extension outside N is made. It preserves plane incidences and the exterior designation since its outer boundary maps to the outer boundary of R0. Indeed complementary paths inside N map inside R0, and excursions outside N can be replaced by paths outside R0, which misses the carrier. Thus the normalized carrier is still finite polygonal and lies in y<=1. Define Q(x,y)=(q(x,y),y): for y<0 put q=x; for 0<=y<=1 put q=sign(x)max(|x|-y,0); for y>1 and |x|<=y put q=(1-1/y)x; for y>1 and |x|>=y put q=x-sign(x). The formulas agree on their seams and extend continuously on the closed plane. Each horizontal line outside T maps strictly monotonically onto the corresponding line minus its collapsed point when 0<=y<=1, or onto the whole line otherwise. The inverse formulas are continuous there; Q is therefore a homeomorphism off T onto the complement of the vertical segment. Only the two sides of T in the carrier are identified. Its complement is deformed, not fixed. On y<=1 the formula is piecewise linear, so the carrier stays polygonal after this fold; no smooth-straightening theorem or extra combinatorial subdivision is hidden. The map is injective on each open face and on every point off the folding arc. Each old characteristic attaching map is composed with Q. The two occupied sides formerly opposite the exterior collar become the opposite sides of the merged edge, never duplicate occurrences on one side. Thus every retained characteristic polygon keeps its whole labelled boundary walk, even when the two sides now belong to the same face. The exterior walk loses precisely the two folded traversals: tracing its empty exterior corner bypasses the matched arc; all other edge-side successors remain unchanged. The unbounded region remains connected: a path entering the removed exterior collar can be rerouted just outside its third side, using its disk chart; no bounded empty region is created. To handle the remaining distinct-edge cases, including loops, parameterize the two complete inverse-labelled occurrences e,f and mark their half-parameter points only geometrically. Never add those marks as graph vertices or labelled half-edges. Use the simple-arc PL collapse twice solely to construct one composite quotient: first on the two subarcs adjacent to the common endpoint, then on the complementary subarcs. The intermediate image is not a labelled diagram and the occurrence invariant is not invoked there. If A!=C, the composite matches e(t) with f(1-t) over the two complete parameter intervals; only then compose characteristic maps, obtaining one whole labelled edge and preserving the shore and exterior-successor invariants. If A=C, the complementary subarcs form an auxiliary embedded circle. Its outside sector at their common midpoint contains no other germ, so the first paired-subarc image and all other incident germs there lie on the bounded side. Delete that circle and its bounded-side carrier, retaining A. This deletes both complete original edge occurrences. Every open face lies wholly inside or outside the circle; a retained face avoids the complete deleted occurrences, while a deleted face is removed whole. Hence no partial labelled edge or relator occurrence exists in the final diagram. If the original two occurrences are the same edge reversed, consecutiveness on both outer shores makes its middle endpoint a leaf, so remove that whole end spur. No operation increases face count or incidence. Contractibility follows with the same characteristic polygons. If a face remains, some face edge meets the unbounded region: follow a generic path from a face to outside the finite graph, and take its last crossing. Such an edge has exactly one face-side occurrence, by the occupied-side invariant. If this face has just one labelled side occurrence, the complementary characteristic boundary is its single marked vertex v. Model its abstract disk by a convex polygon with v on the boundary: extra geometric corners subdivide the parameterization only, not the labelled occurrence. The attaching map is injective on its open disk and on its unique open side, and the free side meets no other face. The disk therefore meets the remainder of the carrier only at the image of v. The affine homotopy H_t(z)=(1-t)z+t v contracts this characteristic disk to v while fixing v. It descends to the carrier and extends by the identity on the remainder, giving the required deformation retraction in this monogon case; no point is mapped to a nontrivial boundary arc. If the face has at least two labelled side occurrences, the complement of the unique open free occurrence is a genuine closed arc in its abstract characteristic boundary, even if its image repeats vertices or edges. In this case map this unique free side to the top side of T0={|x|<=y<=1} by the proved PL disk extension; the other boundary occurrences form the retained two-side arc. The homotopy H_t(x,y)=(x,(1-t)y+t|x|) retracts T0 onto that arc and fixes it pointwise. Conjugate back to the characteristic polygon. All boundary identifications other than the unique free side lie in the fixed retained arc, so this homotopy descends to the attached face even when its boundary repeats vertices or edges, and extends by the identity on the rest of the complex. Removing the open free edge and face therefore gives a deformation retract. That emptied face connects to the exterior through the removed edge; all other bounded regions remain filled. Repeat until only a connected finite graph remains. It has no cycle, since a simple polygonal cycle would bound an unfilled region. It is a tree and contracts by successive leaf retractions. This proves contractibility without assuming nonsingular closed face boundaries. Every completed original-edge cancellation removes two original outer letters, so this finite process reaches the reduced word. Reverse a free reduction of w by attaching exterior spurs at the specified occurrences; this recovers w exactly without faces. A final edge not incident to a face cannot lie on a cycle, since polygon separation would put a filled region against it; it is a bridge and appears twice outside. The face-incident edges number at most I, and thin edges at most n/2, hence E<=I+n<=Lm+n, independently of conjugator lengths. Cayley labels agree at every fold because the two inverse traversals have identical endpoint and intermediate labels; spur labels extend uniquely. In the normalized folding chart use K_0=closure(R_0 minus T_0), omitting the relative interior of the top edge of T_0; its boundary is the simple seven-corner notch polygon and its intersection with T_0 is just the sloping arc. Likewise K=closure(N minus T).

items.title: Controlled coarse triangulation of singular planar diagrams
items.statement: A singular planar diagram supplied by the preceding lemma, with E edges, m faces, outer length n and total face incidence I<=Lm, has a genuine coarse triangulated disk with the original boundary walk up to inserted repetitions, edge bound max(1,L), and at most 16E+4I+4 triangles. Hence with E<=Lm+n it has at most 20(L+1)(m+n+1) triangles, including monogons, bigons, loops, repeated face occurrences and the zero-face cases.
items.strategy: Take the disk-and-band neighbourhood of the embedded graph constructed by lem-finite-polygonal-disk-and-collar-surgery. Every vertex of degree d>=1 has d distinct band attachment intervals and d intervening sectors in cyclic order; a loop uses two intervals. Mark both endpoints and the midpoint of each attachment interval, and the midpoint of each intervening sector. This is a combinatorial 4d-gon, triangulated from an interior center into 4d triangles. Each band has its two end midpoints already marked; also mark the midpoint of each long shore. It is an 8-gon, coned from its own center into 8 triangles. These subdivisions agree exactly along attachments. For each bounded complementary component of the graph, its boundary in the neighbourhood follows one long band shore and one vertex sector for each of its k edge occurrences. Both pieces have two segments, so this is a simple 4k-gon, even when k=1 or 2 or an original vertex/edge occurs repeatedly. Cap it by the polygonal disk lemma and triangulate an abstract 4k-gon by its center, transporting the topological triangulation to the cap; no geometric straight-line fan visibility is assumed. Distinct caps use distinct boundary circles. The preceding diagram lemma fills every bounded graph face; there are therefore exactly the m relator caps, with sum k=I. The union caps all inner boundary components of the graph neighbourhood, and is a genuine closed disk by the disk/collar lemma, not by contractibility alone. Counts are sum_v 4deg(v)=8E, 8E for bands, and 4I for caps, giving 16E+4I. For E=0 take a square with central vertex, four triangles and constant label. Each vertex-disk vertex and center receives its original Cayley vertex label. A band midpoint and center receive either one of that band's endpoint labels, consistently wherever shared; thus all band triangle edges have image length at most one. A cap center receives one of its boundary vertex labels. All cap boundary labels lie along the same relator walk, so every edge from its center has image length at most k<=L; inserting repeated labels adds no distance. The outer boundary has, per original outside edge occurrence, two shore segments whose labels perform that original edge once and a repetition; all intervening vertex sectors are constant. The original cyclic word is therefore retained up to repeated vertices, including bridges and loops. Finally 16E+4I+4<=20Lm+16n+4<=20(L+1)(m+n+1).

items.title: Algebraic relator area controls coarse filling area
items.statement: For a finite presentation with relator lengths at most L, every null edge loop w has a coarse filling with r<=max(1,L) and N<=C(L)(Area(w)+|w|+1). A geodesic triangle of perimeter P in the metric realization admits an approximating edge loop of length <=P+6 with three marked arcs at uniformly bounded Hausdorff distance from the original sides.
items.strategy: First define the unit-edge realization of the earlier simple Cayley graph. Between points in different edge interiors, minimize over the four pairs of edge endpoints the sum of their partial-edge lengths and the integer vertex distance; for points on one edge also allow its direct subinterval. These finitely many attained candidates give the path metric and an isometric minimizing path. This proves geodesicity locally; the published word-metric theorem only concerns vertices. Identity generators map to repeated vertices and collapsed edges. For a null word w, the set of lengths of its finite relator-product expressions is a nonempty subset of N; thm-well-ordering-principle supplies its least member m=Area(w), and choose an expression of that length. The singular-diagram lemma gives E<=Lm+n and the thickening count gives N<=16E+4Lm+4<=20Lm+16n+4<=20(L+1)(m+n+1), so the exported constant is C(L)=20(L+1), independent of conjugator lengths and the number of generators. For each triangle vertex choose one endpoint of its unit edge. Attach connectors of length <=1 on each incident side. Removing the initial and final partial edges leaves an edge path; cancellations at the two connectors change only bounded endpoint pieces. Thus each marked edge path stays within distance <=2 of its original side, and total length <=P+6. Short sides contained in one or two edges are handled by paths of length <=3 near the vertex and a fixed error. The boundary map may have repetitions.

items.title: Polygonal boundary crossing forces coverage by affine triangles
items.statement: Suppose a triangulated disk maps affinely on triangles to R^2 and its three boundary arcs map into the nonnegative coordinate axes (first two arcs, meeting at the origin) and the set max(s,t)>=h (third arc), respectively. The axis endpoints of the third arc lie beyond h. Then the image covers (0,h)^2. The area of a union of N image triangles whose coordinate differences along each edge are at most r is at most Nr^2.
items.strategy: For a point z in the open square away from the finitely many image edges, choose a generic ray from z avoiding all image vertices. Define the signed crossing count of an oriented polygonal loop with this ray. Check directly that a triangle not containing z contributes zero: it enters and exits with opposite signs; a triangle containing z contributes its orientation sign. Sum over coherently oriented domain triangles: internal edge contributions cancel, leaving the boundary count. On the two axes and the exterior of the open square, the boundary loop deforms to the boundary of a rectangle around z without passing z; justify invariance by subdividing a polygonal homotopy into triangles avoiding z and using the same cancellation identity. The boundary count is one, so some image triangle contains z. Points on image edges follow by closedness of the finite union. Each image triangle has determinant area at most r^2 since each coordinate edge difference is <=r. Finite area subadditivity is proved by drawing all supporting edge lines and partitioning into finitely many convex polygonal cells, summing triangle areas. No Jordan curve theorem, degree theorem, integration or unproved planar separation is imported.

items.title: Coarse triangle minsize is bounded by square root of area
items.statement: If a coarse triangular boundary admits an r-edge disk with N triangles, its vertex minsize m satisfies m<=2r sqrt(N)+2r. A continuous boundary lying within Hausdorff distance e of each marked vertex arc has minsize <=2r sqrt(N)+2r+2e.
items.strategy: Map a vertex v to (d(f(v),A_1),d(f(v),A_2)), where A_i are the finite image sets of the first two arcs, and extend affinely. Coordinates are 1-Lipschitz along edges. On the third arc at a vertex, if both coordinates were <m/2, nearest points on A_1,A_2 together with that vertex would have diameter <m. Along any edge, each coordinate changes by <=r, so max(s,t)>=m/2-r throughout that arc. The two other arcs lie on their respective axes; endpoints on the third arc satisfy the same bound. If h=m/2-r>0 the crossing lemma gives area at least h^2; triangle determinants bound it by Nr^2. The nonnegative square root supplied by thm-of-square-roots turns h^2<=Nr^2 into h<=r sqrt(N), giving m<=2r sqrt(N)+2r; if h<=0 the same estimate is automatic. Selecting nearby points of the continuous sides changes a diameter by at most 2e. Retain this discretization term; the sharp inequality quoted in the source is not used without this correction.

items.title: Linear algebraic relator area implies slim Cayley triangles
items.statement: Assume AC. Let a finite presentation have defining relators of length <=L and Area(w)<=K|w| for every null word. Its unit-edge metric Cayley realization has uniformly slim geodesic triangles. More precisely m_X(P)<=A(K,L)sqrt(P+7)+B(L), with finite constants depending only on K,L.
items.strategy: For the approximating edge loop of length n<=P+6, obtain N<=C(L)((K+1)(P+6)+1). The square-root area bound and the bounded boundary error give the asserted common function; e.g. enlarge C(L) and take A=2max(1,L)sqrt(C(L)(K+2)) and B=2max(1,L)+10. Dividing by P tends to zero. Apply the sublinear criterion for this geodesic space. Propagate AC from that criterion. This item alone proves existence for one space; the following independent argument establishes uniformity across presentations.

items.title: Point wedges preserve common triangle minsize bounds
items.statement: Assume AC. Given a countable family of pointed geodesic spaces with m_Xi(P)<=F(P), where F is nonnegative and nondecreasing, their metric wedge at the basepoints is geodesic, each factor is isometrically and geodesically embedded, and m_W(P)<=F(P).
items.strategy: On the disjoint union with roots identified, set cross-factor distance equal to the sum of distances to the roots and retain distances within factors. Check triangle inequalities by inserting the root and the factor triangle inequality. Geodesics between different factors concatenate root segments; a geodesic cannot leave and return to one factor, since that would repeat the root. For triangles with all three vertices in one factor use its bound. With two vertices in one factor, the part there is a triangle with third vertex the root; the other factor contributes tails to two sides, so any minimizing triple of the core triangle remains on the three original sides and its perimeter is at most P. With vertices in three factors, all three sides contain the root and minsize is zero. Root vertices and zero-length sides follow the same cases. Choices of different root geodesics do not matter: in the two-factor case the actual chosen segments define the core triangle, and in the three-factor case the common root still lies on every side. AC selects factor geodesics when proving existence, not the metric formula.

items.title: Filling constants give a uniform slimness bound
items.statement: Assume AC. For every K>=0 and L>=0 there is delta(K,L)<infinity such that every finite presentation with relator lengths <=L and Area(w)<=K|w| for all null words has delta(K,L)-slim triangles in its unit-edge metric Cayley realization. More generally a common nondecreasing sublinear minsize majorant for a countable family forces a common slimness bound.
items.strategy: If there were no common bound, choose for each n a presentation and an actual triangle of slimness >n. Finite presentations can be relabelled by finite subsets of N, so the choice is from a set; AC also supplies the triangles. The preceding linear-area proof gives every factor the same nondecreasing F(P)=A(K,L)sqrt(P+7)+B(L), with F(P)/P tending to zero. Form the point wedge. Its minsize has the same majorant by the wedge lemma, hence the sublinear criterion makes it delta-slim for some finite delta. Each selected triangle is isometrically embedded in the wedge and its side-to-side distances are unchanged, contradicting n>delta. This proves existence of a constant depending only on K,L; it does not claim an explicit numerical formula. The same argument works for an already supplied countable family with any common sublinear majorant.

title: Asymptotic Cones and the Sublinear Triangle Criterion: Examples

items.title: Cones of a line and of real trees
items.statement: Assume AC. The cone of R at any basepoints and scales is isometric to R; every cone of a real tree is a real tree (it need not be the same tree).
items.strategy: The isometry sends [x_n] to lim_omega lambda_n(x_n-e_n); inverse t maps to e_n+t/lambda_n. For a tree, every triangle has minsize zero. The cone-segment lemma makes all cone triangles limit triangles; their branch points have bounded rescaled distance and pass to a common point. Include AC for the geodesic-selection lemma when using it.

items.title: A Euclidean right triangle has minsize proportional to its scale
items.statement: For the triangle with vertices (0,0),(s,0),(0,s), s>0, minsize is at least s/2 and at most s, hence is a positive linear function of s by dilation. Its perimeter is (2+sqrt(2))s.
items.strategy: Use lem-metrics-on-rn for d_2 on R^2 and thm-of-square-roots for sqrt(2). The three displayed sides are the images of the isometric affine parameterizations gamma_1(u)=(u,0), gamma_2(u)=(0,u) for 0<=u<=s, and gamma_3(u)=(u/sqrt(2),s-u/sqrt(2)) for 0<=u<=s sqrt(2): direct subtraction gives d_2(gamma_i(u),gamma_i(v))=|u-v|. Thus their perimeter is (2+sqrt(2))s. Write p=(u,0), q=(0,v), r=(t,s-t) on the three side images. Their diameter is at least each of the distances of r to the two axis sides, namely s-t and t; hence it is at least s/2. Taking p=q=(0,0) and r=(s,0) gives diameter s. Dilation bijects all admissible triples and multiplies every d_2-distance by s, so minsize is exactly s times its positive value at s=1. This does not assert an optimal coefficient.

items.title: Scaling distinguishes sublinear minsize from a fixed perimeter cutoff
items.statement: If m_X(P)=o(P) and lambda_n tends to zero while lambda_n P_n stays bounded, then lambda_n m_X(P_n) tends to zero. A fixed upper bound on P_n also gives zero after rescaling, but says nothing about triangles with P_n of order 1/lambda_n.
items.strategy: For every epsilon choose P0 with m_X(P)<=epsilon P for P>=P0; below P0 use m_X(P)<=P0. Thus lambda_n m_X(P_n)<=epsilon lambda_n P_n+lambda_n P0. Independently of the preceding example, use lem-metrics-on-rn and thm-of-square-roots to parameterize the three sides of the right triangle with vertices (0,0),(n+1,0),(0,n+1) by (u,0), (0,u), and (u/sqrt(2),n+1-u/sqrt(2)); direct subtraction proves that these are d_2-geodesics. The coordinate estimate gives minsize at least (n+1)/2 and perimeter (2+sqrt(2))(n+1), so under lambda_n=1/(n+1) both stay bounded away from zero at every natural index, including zero. This inline witness preserves B-page leaf independence. For a fixed triangle both rescaled perimeter and minsize vanish.
